title: Jeremiah 50:21–32
context: The LORD continues, summoning attackers against Merathaim and Pekod (50:21), lamenting the broken “hammer of the whole earth” (50:23), and opening his armory against the Chaldeans (50:25). Refugees carry news of “the vengeance of his temple” to Zion (50:28), and the LORD declares himself against Babylon, “you proud one” (50:31–32). The names Merathaim and Pekod are often explained as wordplays on Babylonian place or people names; that explanation is held with caution.

verses.text: “Go up against the land of Merathaim, even against it, and against the inhabitants of Pekod. Kill and utterly destroy after them,” says the LORD, “and do according to all that I have commanded you.
verses.arminianNotes: “Go up against the land of Merathaim, even against it, and against the inhabitants of Pekod.” Arminian readers see the LORD commissioning the attack on Babylon as his judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD directing the attack. Many interpreters take Merathaim and Pekod as wordplays on names associated with Babylonia, though readers in this tradition hold those explanations with caution.

verses.text: A sound of battle is in the land, and of great destruction.
verses.arminianNotes: “A sound of battle is in the land, and of great destruction.” Arminian readers see the poem moving into vivid scenes of conflict that announce the city’s coming fall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the noise of battle signaling judgment. Readers in this tradition read the short verse as part of the poem’s rapid, dramatic style, building the sense of urgency.

verses.text: How the hammer of the whole earth is cut apart and broken! How Babylon has become a desolation among the nations!
verses.arminianNotes: “How the hammer of the whole earth is cut apart and broken!” Arminian readers see Babylon, which shattered nations, now shattered itself, showing the limits of human power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the hammer image reversed. Babylon, used to strike others, is broken, and readers in this tradition see God’s sovereignty over even the mightiest empire.

verses.text: I have laid a snare for you, and you are also taken, Babylon, and you weren’t aware. You are found, and also caught, because you have fought against the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “I have laid a snare for you, and you are also taken, Babylon, and you weren’t aware.” Arminian readers see Babylon caught by surprise because it fought against the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD as the one who sets the trap. Readers in this tradition note that the reason given is Babylon’s fighting against the LORD, so its fall is just judgment.

verses.text: The LORD has opened his armory, and has brought out the weapons of his indignation; for the Lord, GOD of Armies, has a work to do in the land of the Chaldeans.
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD has opened his armory, and has brought out the weapons of his indignation.” Arminian readers see the nations used against Babylon pictured as weapons in God’s hand.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD as a warrior with a work to do. Readers in this tradition see the attacking nations as instruments in his hand, while 50:29 still grounds the judgment in Babylon’s own pride.

verses.text: Come against her from the farthest border. Open her storehouses. Cast her up as heaps. Destroy her utterly. Let nothing of her be left.
verses.arminianNotes: “Come against her from the farthest border. Open her storehouses.” Arminian readers see the call to strip Babylon of its accumulated wealth, a reversal of its own plundering.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see judgment on Babylon’s riches. The language of utter destruction is stark, and readers in this tradition read it soberly as prophetic war poetry announcing God’s verdict.

verses.text: Kill all her bulls. Let them go down to the slaughter. Woe to them! For their day has come, the time of their visitation.
verses.arminianNotes: “Kill all her bulls. Let them go down to the slaughter.” Arminian readers commonly take the bulls as a figure for Babylon’s strong men or leaders, whose day of reckoning has come.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise take the bulls as figurative, probably for the city’s warriors. The phrase “their day has come, the time of their visitation” marks the appointed time of judgment.

verses.text: Listen to those who flee and escape out of the land of Babylon, to declare in Zion the vengeance of the LORD our God, the vengeance of his temple.
verses.arminianNotes: “Listen to those who flee and escape out of the land of Babylon, to declare in Zion the vengeance of the LORD.” Arminian readers see exiles returning with news of God’s justice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see refugees proclaiming “the vengeance of his temple.” Readers in this tradition note that Babylon’s destruction of the temple is remembered as part of the cause of judgment.

verses.text: “Call together the archers against Babylon, all those who bend the bow. Encamp against her all around. Let none of it escape. Pay her back according to her work. According to all that she has done, do to her; for she has been proud against the LORD, against the Holy One of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: “Pay her back according to her work … for she has been proud against the LORD, against the Holy One of Israel.” Arminian readers see pride named as the root of Babylon’s guilt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see pride against the Holy One as Babylon’s central sin. The title “the Holy One of Israel” is frequent in Isaiah, and readers in this tradition see its use here as stressing God’s holiness offended.

verses.text: Therefore her young men will fall in her streets. All her men of war will be brought to silence in that day,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore her young men will fall in her streets.” Arminian readers see the judgment falling on Babylon’s fighting men, as it had once fallen on Jerusalem’s, read soberly and without delight.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the reversal of Jerusalem’s fate. The same words appear against Damascus in 49:26, and readers in this tradition note the reuse of such lines across the oracles against the nations.

verses.text: “Behold, I am against you, you proud one,” says the Lord, GOD of Armies; “for your day has come, the time that I will visit you.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, I am against you, you proud one,” says the Lord, GOD of Armies. Arminian readers see Babylon personified as “proud one,” facing the LORD himself as its opponent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s personal opposition to pride. Readers in this tradition commonly relate this to the wider biblical theme of God humbling the proud, which runs through these oracles.

verses.text: The proud one will stumble and fall, and no one will raise him up. I will kindle a fire in his cities, and it will devour all who are around him.”
verses.arminianNotes: “The proud one will stumble and fall, and no one will raise him up.” Arminian readers see pride leading to a fall from which there is no human rescue.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the certainty of the proud one’s fall. The fire kindled in its cities pictures complete judgment, and readers in this tradition see the LORD as the one who brings down the arrogant.
